Everyone knows AI agents exist.
But no one knows how to use them.

So I spent 300+ hours testing GTM agents.

These are the 7 agents that will actually help you find more clients:

1/ Research agent: Claygent

↳ Helps you perform deep prospect research at scale.

Claygent is like hiring a researcher who never sleeps.

Ask it to “find pricing info for 100 SaaS tools,” and it will:

• Crawl websites
• Locate pricing pages
• Summarize key plans
• Show how it found each data point

Over 1 billion runs later, Claygent remains my go-to agent for deep and scalable prospect insights.

2/ 'Reply' agent: Instantly

↳ Monitors your inbox and crafts replies on your behalf.

We use Instantly's reply agent internally.

If you've sent cold outreach at scale, you might've noticed that:
faster replies = more meetings booked.

You can train 24/7 reply agents that autonomously:
- analyze reply sentiment (positive vs. negative)
- draft a personalized answer mimicking your voice

It can be run on autopilot, but I recommend keeping a human in the loop.

3/ Sales agent: Attention

↳ Extracts relevant insights from your sales conversations.

We use Attention to record, transcribe & take notes from meetings.

Then, Attention's AI analyzes convos to:
- suggest follow-ups or next steps
- point out recurring patterns
- update the CRM

I use it to analyze 100+ conversations at a time to get answers to questions such as:
- what objections are preventing prospects from buying
- where did prospects first hear about us
- what problems are they willing to solve
- what led them to booking a meeting

4/ Sourcing agent: Exa

↳ Helps you source precise lead lists, fast.

My favourite example is Exa's websets.

You ask, in natural language, who you're looking for:

i.e: "CEO at AI companies, from 20 to 50 employees, in California, who raised > $5 million"

The agent independently understands what filtering criteria to use and finds your ideal leads.

5/ LinkedIn agent: Valley

↳ Acts as your LinkedIn SDRs.

Valley is a great demonstration of this.

It independently:
- finds ICP fit leads
- craft personalized outreach
- monitors conversations & handles replies

6/ Scraping agent: Apify

↳ Lets you extract data online, at scale.

Apify has a store featuring 200+ pre-built actors, specifically designed to scrape individual platforms.

7/ AI SDR: Artisan

↳ They replace your SDRs.

AI SDRs, like Artisan, operate very similarly to Cold email agencies.

Their goal is to generate results for (many) orgs.

However, where agencies focus on training skilled humans to deliver the work, AI SDR companies 'train' software.

As a rule of thumb, when you outsource to AI, it's always worth allocating extra time to check the output. AI can hallucinate, and these solutions are not yet perfect.

But I want to grow these numbers further. Here's why:

↳ Just last month, we added $89,000+ MRR from new 13 deals. LinkedIn was responsible for 8 of them. And I’d argue it positively influenced the remaining 5.

Having multiple people share their POV on LinkedIn exposes prospects to so many content pieces… that by the time they talk to our sales team, they’re already half sold.

Last month, we collectively published 233 posts. The goal is to reach 500 by the end of this year.

Here’s what’s worked best for us in 2025:

1. Leverage platforms like Taplio for content ideation

It lets you find publications that outperformed.

It’s the fastest way to understand what ‘good’ posts look like for LinkedIn.

Study hooks, frameworks, formats, and CTAs of all these posts.

Re-use the structure of these ‘winning’ publications, and apply them to your niche.

2. Engaging with other creators

LinkedIn pushes you much more when you actively comment on others’ posts.

Last year, I read an experiment where someone:

- Only commented for a couple of weeks
- Only posted for 2 weeks
- Posted & commented

Obviously, posting & commenting together drove the most profile views and follower growth.

But, interestingly, commenting alone earned them more followers than just posting.

Try commenting under posts from large creators, and look at the impression metrics. These might be higher than on any of your posts.

Also, to boost your posts, try this:

- Comment on others’ posts 30 min before hitting ‘publish’
- Reply to every comment you get within the first 30 minutes.

3. Create scroll-stopping visuals

Visuals occupy lots of space on the LinkedIn feed.

This significantly improves the odds that people will read your posts.

Selfies, schemas, infographics, carousels… all these will multiply the reach of your posts.

We’re making it as easy as possible for our team.

4. Repurposing your best hits

Every couple of months: Have a look at your best-performing posts… and rewrite them slightly better.

Have a look at the biggest LinkedIn content creators.

Check their most viral posts.

You’ll notice, they’ve published them over and over…
And they keep performing!

Most viewers forget your posts. But new followers never saw them.

So take your best post ever and publish it again.

We've sent over 23M cold emails and built GTM systems for 300+ B2B companies at $7M ARR.

Here's how the top 1% make cold email work in 2026:
(Based on 1,000,000+ emails analyzed via @InstantlyAI)

1. Small Targeted Lists > Big Broad Lists

> Micro-lists of 500-1,000 hyper-targeted prospects beat blasting 100,000 contacts every time. Reply rates: 20-30% vs. 2-3%.
> Stop praying someone bites. Start targeting the actual people who have a reason to reply.

2. Hyperenriched Data > Basic Data

Go beyond name + email. Collect:

> LinkedIn headline & profile
> Job postings (signals growth/hiring needs)
> Technologies used
> Funding announcements
> Website case studies
> Department & industry
> Company size & connections

Personalization at scale requires data at scale.

3. AI Personalization > Generic Openers

Instead of: "Hey John, hope all is well at [Company]"
Try:

> Job postings → "Saw you're hiring 3 AEs..."
> Funding news → "Congrats on the $25M Series B..."
> Case studies → "Just read your case study on..."
> Tech stack → "Noticed you recently added [tool]..."
> Product launches → "Saw you rolled out 5 new SKUs..."

Make every email feel 1:1.

4. 4-Step Sequence > 1 Single Email

Most replies come from the first emails, but follow-ups increase overall sequence reply rates significantly.

> Email 1: Personalized opener + value offer
> Email 2: Short follow-up (3-5 days later)
> Email 3: Different angle (3-5 days later)
> Email 4: Breakup email (3-5 days later)

Keep them short. 2-4 sentences. Reference the original. Add new value.

Pro tip: Layer in LinkedIn touches between emails for omnipresence.

5. Value-First > Ask-First

Stop asking for their time immediately.

❌ "Can we hop on a call tomorrow at 2pm?"
❌ "Do you have 15 minutes to chat?"

✅ "Would it make sense to send over a quick example deck?"
✅ "Happy to share what's working best right now."
✅ "Can I send you something that could help [specific pain]?"

They raise their hand first. Then you've earned the conversation.

6. Fundamentals > Fancy Tactics

Master the 3 core pillars:

> ICP – Who exactly are you targeting?
> Offer – What specific outcome do you deliver?
> Copy – How do you communicate value?

Depth > Width. No shiny object syndrome.

7. Long Game > Quick Wins

Cold email isn't a magic pill. It's a compounding client acquisition system.
Quality over rushing. Pipeline over quick wins. Be there when they're ready to buy.

8. Deliverability > Volume

None of this matters if you land in spam.

> Multiple domains (not just one)
> 30 emails per inbox per day max
> Proper technical setup (SPF, DKIM, DMARC)
> 30 days minimum warm-up
> Clean, validated lists

Sending 100 emails/hour from one email = spam city.

The biggest lie in cold outreach: more emails = more leads.

We generated 25,000+ leads in 2026 at ColdIQ ($7M ARR). The difference was targeting and tiering, not blasting bigger lists.

1. Segment before you send anything. Companies engaging with your brand, lookalikes of your best clients, and companies showing buying intent in your category. These are the easy targeting wins most teams overlook when they start cold outreach.

2. Map your entire TAM through @clay, Wiza, and @prospeo_io. Then research every account and split them into three tiers. Your dream clients (Tier 1), strong fits (Tier 2), and everyone else you can genuinely help (Tier 3).

3. Each tier gets a completely different outreach motion. Tier 1 is manual AE outreach, one by one: phone (we use Nooks), LinkedIn, and email. Tier 2 is personalized multichannel through @clay + @lemlist. Tier 3 is your experimental playground through @InstantlyAI where you test copywriting frameworks at scale.

4. Write 25-50 messages by hand before automating a single one. The early replies teach you patterns that no template will give you. This step feels slow. It saves months later.

5. Lead with free value, not an ask. For Tier 2, I think about what's the first thing I'd do if I signed them as a client, then I do it already, for free. Example: building a niche lead list with companies and people data of their ideal clients.

Reply speed determines your pipeline. Every hour between their positive response and your follow-up costs you meetings.

Content scales like engineering. Most teams treat it as creative work and the voice converges by month two. We solved this with a per-person system loaded before every generation.

The pipeline runs 27 skills across eight stages, all in one terminal. One folder per person. A grading rubric refuses to ship anything below a /38.

Layer 1: Foundation (built once per person)

Every AI content engine I've audited fails at the same point. By month two, the voice drifts toward whatever the base model considers good business writing. Readers unfollow.

One folder per human, loaded before every generation:

• A voice profile built from a 25-question spoken conversation
• An ICP doc split into three buyer tiers, each with its own language map
• A content pillars file locking the person's three to five themes

The voice profile is the highest-leverage file. We build it from a recorded call. How does the person describe what they do at a dinner. What words do they refuse to use. What phrases do they reach for when explaining something technical to a non-technical buyer. The transcript becomes ground truth, and every draft is compared against it.

The pillars file is the final gate. If a draft doesn't deposit into one of the three to five themes, the system rejects the idea before it becomes a draft.

Layer 2: Research (six workers, every week)

Six workers run weekly and drop a ranked idea batch into each person's folder by Monday morning.

• Apify browses LinkedIn for what's performing in the niche right now.
• Reddit mines the communities our buyers live in for raw, unedited audience language.
• YouTube feeds through Gemini for multimodal video analysis, turning long-form video into pillar-mapped frameworks.
• X surfaces the live ICP debates and the contrarian angle worth taking.
• Fireflies transcripts are the highest-signal source. Clients describe their problems in their own language on diagnostic calls, and that language becomes hooks unedited.
• Repurposing archive indexes everything we've produced so nothing accidentally repeats.

A seventh skill, reverse engineering, runs on demand. It scrapes top niche posts and maps reusable templates back into the hook and copy skills.

Each idea arrives pre-tagged with hook, pillar, and source. Nobody argues about what to post.

Layer 3: Production line (hook → copy → grader)

Four skills, each does one job, hands cleanly to the next.

Hook generator. 50 templates organised by emotional trigger across desire, curiosity, and fear. Each idea produces 20+ hook variations. Underperforming templates get deprecated.

Copy developer. Takes the winning hook and writes a draft in the person's documented voice, loading voice profile, ICP tier, matched pillar, and research snippets.

Visual brief generator. Produces a structured layout plus exact copy placement for the designer. Gemini handles first-pass visuals; Figma and Canva sit above for refinement.

Post grader. Scores every draft on five dimensions: hook strength, voice fit, specificity of claims, scannability, pillar relevance. /50 ceiling. /38 floor. Anything below 38 auto-rewrites with the failing dimension flagged. Nothing ships under a 38.

AI drafts; the human sharpens. The voice profile is the guardrail.

Layer 4: Repurpose (one post, six surfaces)

The repurpose skill rebuilds a validated LinkedIn post into an X thread, an X long-form article with a cover placard, a newsletter, an SEO blog post, a YouTube video script, and a carousel of sequential visual slides. Each destination gets a native rebuild with native formatting, opening patterns, and a CTA that fits the surface.

Voice profile and ICP tier carry over unchanged. Only the structural grammar of the destination shifts.

Feedback capture auto-logs every session: what ran, what the human kept verbatim, what got rewritten, what the grader rejected. System check runs before every production round across Apify, Fireflies, Gemini, Reddit, YouTube, and Claude.

ClickUp is the client-handoff surface. Every approved draft, visual brief, and grader scorecard lands in the client's ClickUp board, where the human can edit, approve, or kick back. Taplio queues approved posts at the right time slot per person and per pillar. Top performers train the hook templates. Underperformers feed the rubric. The loop closes.

Most founders quit LinkedIn after six months. They write technically correct posts, get a handful of likes from coworkers, and decide B2B buyers don't live on the platform.

B2B buyers do live there. They scroll past 200 posts a day and most of those posts get less than a second of consideration before the scroll continues.

I sat down with @PierreReddot (runs Content Path, one of the most-followed B2B marketing creators on LinkedIn) to pull apart what makes a post survive that first second. We've installed a version of his anatomy across 24+ ColdIQ profiles. LinkedIn drives 65% of our inbound and added $80K+ MRR on its own.

A few things actually moved the needle:

1. The image does 95% of the work. The visual is what stops the scroll, what gets screenshotted into a Notes app for next Thursday's meeting, what gets reposted with a one-line caption from someone else's profile. We design the visual first now and write the copy around whatever it's doing.

2. The high-performing posts almost all collapse into one of four archetypes: the comparative table, the pyramid, the iceberg, or the visual metaphor. Pierre's most-copied post pairs a glowing button labelled "what people think marketing is" against a Rubik's cube labelled "what marketing actually is." Pick one archetype and run it across different topics. The reason most accounts plateau is they try to invent a new visual every week instead of building muscle memory on one.

3. The hook has one job. Open a curiosity gap in the first two lines, then pay it off in the line right after "see more." Pierre's name for the most common failure mode is the "deceiving hook," which promises something in line one and resolves it fifteen lines down. It kills more posts than weak openings ever do.

4. Most bodies fail because they read as dense walls of text. We keep posts inside 140 words and 1,300 characters and we vary sentence length deliberately. A six-word punch sits next to a twenty-word analytical sentence, which sits next to a one-word emphasis. The eye needs the rhythm or it bounces.

5. The metric that actually moves the algorithm is saves. Saves correlate with dwell time, and dwell time is what LinkedIn watches across the first 72 hours after publication. We roughly doubled our save rate after three changes: we embedded tool logos like Clay, Lemlist, Apollo, and HubSpot inside the infographic so readers save the post for the stack, we made the framework self-contained enough that a screenshot of the image alone delivers the playbook, and we added one small animated element per post which pushes average dwell from about two seconds to seven.

Most LinkedIn advice is about output. Post cadence, time of day, hashtag strategy, tagging peers. None of it matters if your individual post can't survive a half-second scroll.

Build the anatomy at the unit level first. The volume conversation comes after.

@max_trigify (founder of Trigify) just moved his whole lead gen stack from OpenClaw to Hermes Agent. I got him on a call to break down what he optimized for. Five lessons most operators get wrong:

1. An agent you can't maintain is a liability

OpenClaw is powerful, but if you're not deeply technical it's a part-time job: constant fixing, rewiring, updating every release. Hermes ran out of the box and he hasn't fixed it once. An agent you have to babysit costs more than it saves.

2. Memory is what compounds

This is the real difference. OpenClaw forgets between sessions. Hermes has a self-learning loop:

> Auto-creates skills
> Auto-creates memory files
> Auto-updates them from how you actually work

Max kept asking for stats in his LinkedIn hooks. Hermes saved that as a preference and started writing them that way on its own. No "remember this" prompt. An agent that remembers your preferences compounds; one that forgets makes you re-explain your setup every session.

3. Make one agent the orchestrator

He didn't throw OpenClaw away. On setup, Hermes offers to port your OpenClaw config across, so he kept OpenClaw for the tool-heavy execution and made Hermes the layer that runs everything.

> Hermes = architect, ~90% of the work
> OpenClaw = tool-heavy jobs, ~10%

Most of the time the play is to put one agent in charge of the tools you already use.

4. Keep the model swappable

Anthropic banned third-party tools like OpenClaw from the Max plan, and for him Opus quality dropped. So he swapped to Codex on the $200 plan, and inside Hermes he can't tell Opus 4.6 and GPT 5.4 apart. Build your setup so the model is a part you can change. When one degrades or gets cut off, you swap it and keep running.

5. Structure your memory as a graph

The build detail worth copying. Inspired by Karpathy's note on agent memory, Max runs Hermes's memory in Obsidian as a Wikipedia-style graph. Every concept links to the others: founder-led content links to signal-based selling, which links to brand intelligence. The agent reads across the whole graph before it answers, so every output is informed by everything it knows.

Claude does not read your skill folder on every message. It reads in three layers, and only the first one is always there.

Level 1 is the name and the description. Around 100 tokens per skill, sitting in the system prompt from startup. That is the index card Claude matches your request against.

Level 2 is the body of SKILL.md, the steps and the output shape. Usually under 5k tokens. It only enters context once the description matches what you asked.

Level 3 is anything heavy you bundle: a long API reference, a schema, a script. Claude opens those only when a step points at them. A script Claude runs never loads its code, only its output.

So the name and description carry the entire trigger surface. Everything else stays invisible until those two lines match.

Which is why most first skills die on the description. It gets written about the feature, when the job is to name the moment:

→ "Enriches company data using multiple providers"... sits in the folder
→ "Use when the user gives a company name or URL and wants a research brief before outreach"... gets picked up

Two rules there that are easy to miss.

Write it in third person. That line goes straight into the system prompt, so "I can help you research companies" lands in a different voice than everything around it, and discovery suffers for it.

And spend the characters. You get 1024. A one-line feature summary wastes most of them.

The same design is why a folder full of skills barely costs you anything on a normal message. Until one fires, its name and description are all that occupy context.

So you keep adding them. We run seven master skills now across Clay, cold email, LinkedIn Ads, LinkedIn content, list building, n8n and signal sourcing. Each routes to its own sub-skills, so I ask for an outcome and the system picks the steps.

This is the GTM funnel behind ColdIQ, every layer & the tools that run each one (it books us 100+ meetings a month)

Top to bottom:

1. Traffic

Five channels feed the top. LinkedIn posts, cold outbound, YouTube, X & the blog.

40,000+ people a month land on our website. The biggest sources: the blog and the rest of our AEO & SEO ~12,000 visits/mo, LinkedIn ~10,000 with 10+ of us publishing, cold outbound ~3,000. (YouTube is the one I keep failing to stay consistent on.)

@prospeo_io and @FullEnrich do the enrichment up here, @predictleads for the buying signal, taplio(.)com the post inspiration.

2. The four surfaces

Company page, LinkedIn profile, the website, form fills. Every capture surface we own is one of those four.

3. The eight buckets underneath them

→ page followers, pulled with getleads(.)io
→ connections, profile viewers, post engagers & DMs, all covered by @expandi_io
→ website visitors, caught with vector(.)co, Warm & posthog(.)com, including the ones who never fill anything in
→ newsletter subs in beehiiv(.)com
→ demo bookings through default(.)com, ColdIQ & attio(.)com

Eight streams, eight different shapes, and plenty of the same people showing up across them.

4. Data routing

All eight land in one place. ColdIQ sits there and holds one row per human, so someone who followed the page in spring and booked a demo in summer stops being two separate records.

It dedupes, enriches, timestamps, and keeps the origin bucket. Keep that last one forever, it's what eventually tells you which source was worth funding.

5. Lead scoring & prioritization

Claude Code and Codex do the modelling, ColdIQ holds the records, PredictLeads brings the intent signal.

Train on closed-won first. Those are the accounts you actually want more of. Then feed it closed-lost, so it learns which good-looking accounts never close. Skip the lost deals and everything scores well.

6. Three motions, picked by the score

→ Automated outreach. Email & LinkedIn sequences through @InstantlyAI and @lemlist. Mid score, good fit, unclear timing. Most of the volume ends up living here.

→ Manual sell-by-chat. Email, call, DM, text through Gmail, LinkedIn & nooks(.)ai. High score with live intent, a human the same day. It stays deliberately small, it costs real rep hours per contact.

→ Marketing. Ad retargeting & nurture sequences through LinkedIn, Google & customer(.)io, holding frequency until something in the score moves.

Nothing is permanently assigned. Re-score on every event and people move lanes on their own.

7. Sales process, closed deal

70% of deals are sales-led, usually 1 to 2 calls on Google Meet depending on package size. I record them with claap(.)io and turn them into coaching, cobl(.)ai drafts the proposals off the transcripts.

That's the map, and it reads top to bottom.

You build it middle out. Start dead centre with the router, then scoring, then the lanes, then work back up to claim the eight buckets, and open the channels last. Build it the other way round and everything above the router is collecting records that nothing can join up.

You can be everywhere on an account. Inbox, LinkedIn notifications, phone, even something physical at the door if the deal is big enough.

Most teams pick one of those and then talk about outbound being difficult in 2026. Treat outbound as a single channel activity, and you will struggle with generating pipeline.

Or you could do multi-channel outbound, and book far more meetings.

Here's how to segment channels and run multi-channel the right way:

- Email scales further than anything else. It's also crowded and deliverability-sensitive, so it takes the widest lists & the least personalization per send.
- LinkedIn almost always gets delivered and read on mobile, but you're capped on actions per day. Use it where an actual relationship is the goal.
- Phone is hard to scale and most people won't pick up. The ones who do convert better than anything else here, so tier 1 only.
- In person & gifts, completely unscalable, highest signal of them all. Only for the handful where deal size covers it.

Then route by tier. You never run all four channels at one account:

Tier 3 → email
Tier 2 → email + LinkedIn
Tier 1 → email, LinkedIn, then the call, in that order

Tier 2 runs as one sequence with a single branch:
email → profile visit → connection invite → check after a day. If they accepted, message them on LinkedIn. If not, follow-up email.

Fit tells you who. These signals tell you when:
new hire, job change, hiring for a role, a new exec at a customer account, profile visitor. Profile visitor is the warmest of the five, they looked at you first.

"Congrats on the 5 years at [company]" proves you read a profile field.

"You said on the podcast you're rebuilding the SDR team" is the reason you're writing today. Self-authored > company > role.

When someone asks me which channel books more meetings, cold email, LinkedIn DMs or cold calling, my first question back is what the account is worth.

You rank the accounts first, and the channel follows from the tier. We've run outbound for 275+ companies and that's genuinely the whole answer.

Here's how the split works:

1. Tier the accounts before you pick a channel

Tier 1 = dream accounts, manual and high touch. They get your DM slots and your call blocks.

Tier 2 and 3 = the scale plays. They go to the email engine, where the TAM is broad enough that testing at volume makes sense.

The allocation mistake we see most often: teams spending their 100 weekly DM slots on tier 3 contacts a mailbox could have handled.

2. Check what each channel can physically carry

→ LinkedIn: ~100 DMs or connection requests a week, platform enforced. Push past it and you risk an account you spent years building.

→ Email: ~25 sends per mailbox per day before spam risk climbs. Mailboxes stack though, so 10 of them is about 1,250 a week (one number is the per-mailbox threshold, the other is a full sending setup).

→ Calling: 50 to 100 dials per rep per day. A parallel dialer lifts the connects you get out of those hours, but you're still buying capacity in rep time, which is the most expensive kind.

So a market of thousands of contacts can't be worked over DMs, and 200 named accounts gain nothing from a 1,250-send week.

3. On tier 1, run all three in order

week 1: connect + a real comment, no ask
week 1-2: DM with something useful in it, zero pitch
week 2: email with the substance, one clear CTA
week 3: call, referencing the thread you've already built

A funding round is a 10-point signal.

A fresh pricing-page visit can enter the 80+ band.

Those are starter weights. Your reply and meeting data should tune them.

Most teams work them the other way around: they automate the public announcement every competitor can see, then let the strongest intent die inside a dashboard.

The signal alone is not the entire system. You still have to decide what matters, how long it matters and what a rep should do next.

Here is the starter model I use (that you can copy too): 

Only track signals your offer can act on.

Budget-gated product → funding, leadership hire, expansion.

Replacement product → tool added or dropped, review-site activity, competitor ad shifts.

Role-attached product → job openings, champion moves, team growth.

Self-serve product → product usage, pricing-page visits, content engagement.

Pick three from the relevant row. Do not add a fourth until those three produce meetings.

Score the full account.

Start with:

First-party signal: 40 points
Second-party signal: 25 points
Third-party signal: 10 points
Then apply four modifiers:
×2 when the signal is inside its freshness window
+15 when signals from 2+ tiers stack on one account
+10 when the signal resolves to the actual buyer
−20 when the same event was counted twice

That last rule matters. A round surfaced by PredictLeads, Crunchbase and a news monitor is one event. Count it once.

Suppress before a rep sees the queue.
Remove open opportunities, active sequences and anyone touched in the last 14 days. Then enrich the accounts that survive with the person who actually owns the problem.
Let the score determine the treatment.
80+ → work today, manually. DM or call.

40 to 79 → sequence this week with the context built in.

Below 40 → nurture. Wait for another signal.

If 400 accounts hit the manual band, the model is not calibrated. Raise the threshold until the queue matches the team’s actual capacity.

Expire every signal.

Hours → pricing-page visit, demo form, product-usage spike.

Days → content download, ad engagement, LinkedIn engagement.

1 to 2 weeks → job post, champion move, review-site visit.

2 to 6 weeks → funding round. Skip week one, when every vendor is sending congratulations.

Months → technographic change, leadership hire, expansion.

The fastest-decaying signals tend to convert best. They also punish slow operations the hardest.

Use the signal to choose the situation without exposing the surveillance.

Funding → the hiring plan or target the money created.

Job opening → the work behind the role.

Tool added → the adjacent gap it creates.

Tool dropped → what broke badly enough to make them leave.

Pricing-page visit → say nothing. Use it only for timing and priority.

Build the first version with what you already own.

Start the merge with the owned inputs already available: call transcripts, CRM activity, form fills and website visitors. Activate only the three categories that pass the offer-fit filter above, then pull them into one spreadsheet.

Keep one row per company, deduped by domain, with signal type, tier, source, timestamp, score, buyer, last touch and outcome.

That is enough for the first 100 target accounts.

Run it by hand and tag every outcome back to its source. Each month, track signals surfaced, signals actioned, action rate, reply rate, meetings, cost and cost per meeting.

Pause any source that produces zero actioned signals for two months.

For one quarter, give one owner three categories and one spreadsheet.

The replies and meetings decide which categories earned their place, and whether a fourth deserves to be added.

This exact LinkedIn content process generated ~20M impressions for our team in one year.

Many GTM agencies in our space felt my content was "too basic." Good. I wasn't writing for other GTM agency founders. I wanted revenue leaders (aka my ICP) consuming it.

Considering it helped us add $4M in net ARR, I think we were writing for the right people.

If you want to replicate this, here's the RIGHT way to do it:

1. Get specific about who your buyer is.

For us, that's the person responsible for pipeline. They want to understand why their campaigns aren't getting replies & what they can change.

Write down the questions they ask, the problems they're trying to fix, and what they need to understand before hiring you. Those are your starting topics.

2. Work out who would share it with them.

Your buyer might be a VP of Sales. But the person discovering your content could be an SDR on their team.

So, make something that SDR can use. A campaign template, for example, or a breakdown they can forward to their manager. You can still reach the buyer this way.

3. Review what's already been produced.

Look at your own best posts, your competitors' content, and the industry voices your buyers follow.

Compare the topics, examples, hooks and visuals. Does someone know more than you, or are they better at explaining what they know?

Use that research to build your next batch of ideas. A post that worked before can become a follow-up, a more detailed tutorial, or a breakdown with a fresh example.

4. Build a swipe file of formats you can reuse.

Taplio helps you find outlier posts in your niche. Save the hook structure, the way the information is organised & the visual treatment.

Add a note on how you'd apply each format to your own topic. You still need your own examples and experience.

5. Pick 2-3 topics & 2-3 formats to keep using.

For us, that can mean cold email systems and GTM stacks, packaged as breakdowns or infographics.

Keep improving those combinations. You don't need a new subject every week. New people are discovering your account, and they haven't read everything you've published.

6. Give people different reasons to read you.

Here's what you can actually post at each stage:

To reach new people (TOF): hot takes, build-in-public updates, thought leadership, personal stories and giveaways.

To help them understand your expertise (MOF): how-to tutorials, frameworks, playbooks, checklists and "how I did it" transformations.

To help them decide whether to buy (BOF): promotional offers, testimonials, customer success stories, product demos and answers to frequently asked questions.

Take cold email as an example. You could share your take on why campaigns get ignored, teach readers how to diagnose one, then show a real customer result from fixing that problem.

Make room for all three stages in your calendar.

7. Interview the people doing the work & build the visual.

Ask the founder or team member: What was the problem? What did you change? What happened? Can we show it?

Choose the visual that explains it: a workflow diagram, a checklist, a screenshot or a demo. Our designer uses Claude Code + Figma for our infographics.

Then use the interview material to write the caption around it. A tutorial needs the actual steps. A success story needs the result and enough context to understand it.

8. Put the posts on a calendar & publish them.

For each post, write down the topic, format, funnel stage, example, visual and publication date.

If you've planned nothing but hot takes, add a tutorial or checklist. If every post asks people to buy, add something useful they can apply before becoming a customer.

Publish, answer comments, and open conversations with relevant engagers. Handle the enquiries that come in; the content doesn't do the sales work for you.

I recently spoke to a video agency founder about improving his LinkedIn content and using it to attract buyers.

During a content exercise, he showed me a viral post he liked and wanted to replicate.

But copying its hook and framing would have told his own buyers they didn't need his agency in the first place.

He'd picked it because he liked the visual. But the hook positioned Claude Code as a replacement for the service he was trying to sell.

So we kept the visual concept and changed the angle: how his agency could use Claude Code to deliver better videos on smaller budgets. Same source of inspiration, now giving buyers a reason to hire him.

Here's how to work out which parts of a viral post you can use for your own business:

1. Find an outlier, then check what you're comparing it against.

Look at the author's surrounding posts. You're looking for something that performed unusually well for that account. A big like count on a huge account tells you very little on its own.

In the session, I used Scripe to search relevant keywords and filter by date and likes. Start with your niche, then look at adjacent ones for formats you could explain through your own expertise.

2. Open the original post and separate its parts.

Save the hook, the supporting line, the body structure, the proof, the visual and the CTA.

Check whether the post was edited. In our example, the updated copy pointed to a resource. I thought the lead magnet helped drive the engagement; the graphic wasn't the whole explanation.

Read the comments too. Are people discussing the idea, asking for the resource or arguing with the claim? Those are different reasons for a post to take off.

3. Translate the idea into a problem your buyer has.

"Claude Code for marketing" could become "Claude Code for video."

But "AI replaces video agencies" would undermine what he sells. And "small agencies can compete with bigger agencies" would interest his peers.

His clients cared about production quality and budget. So we discussed an angle about using Claude Code to improve production on smaller budgets.

Before writing, finish this sentence: "The person who would hire us wants to know how to ___."

4. Supply the knowledge the original format leaves out.

A list of prompts might work in one niche. Video production also needs context: product images, existing footage, brand material and visual references.

If your reader needs those inputs to use the advice, explain them before the prompts.

Build the body from work you can show. For each example, include the input, what you did, the output and anything that still needed a person to fix it. Use your own results as proof; don't inherit the original author's numbers.

5. Write the hook and sub-hook together.

The hook gives the reader a specific reason to open the post. The next line handles the obvious objection or explains what they'll get.

For a video-production tutorial, that could be:

"AI prompts for product videos."
"Including the source images and reference shots each prompt needs."

Then deliver those materials in the body. If you promise usable prompts, show tested prompts. If you promise better production quality, show the work that supports it.

6. Rebuild the visual around your version.

In this case, I suggested adapting the image concept into "Claude Code for video" while dropping the replacement pitch.

You can borrow a comparison layout, a list structure or a workflow diagram. Replace its examples, labels and supporting material with your own. Keep only the parts that help someone understand your subject.

7. Make the next action fit what you delivered.

A useful discussion needs a question someone can answer from experience. A resource offer needs a finished resource you can send. A service CTA should explain what you can implement for the reader.

If you're looking to automate your GTM using Claude Code, here's the right way to do it:

1. Know what you're actually automating.

Almost every tool in your stack is a login screen wrapped around an API. Apollo is a contact database with a search bar bolted on. Smartlead is a deliverability engine with the sequence builder as the wrapper.

What you pay for is the API underneath, & a coding agent calls it directly.

Go down your billing page and check which of them publish API docs. That set is what you can drive from a terminal on day one, and the clicking, exporting and copy-pasting between them stops there.

2. Write the context folder before you touch a single API key.

Four plain markdown files. No formatting rules, nobody but the agent reads them:

icp.md: who you sell to, the 3-4 attributes that separate an account that replies from one that doesn't, and your disqualifiers. Company size, the tools they run, who they hired last quarter.

results.md: every campaign you've run, the list definition behind it, the angle, and the reply rate. Keep the losers in. They're what stops the agent proposing them again.

angles.md: the offers and hooks that landed, each one tagged with the segment it landed on.

sop.md: how you run a campaign start to finish, in the order you actually do it.

The test to run once done with this step: can you name the last 3 campaigns that worked & why they worked?

If you can't, neither can the agent, so it builds the broadest list it can.

3. Do the boring mapping the demos skip.

A TAM map is the full list of accounts you'd be happy to close, before any filtering. An ICP Matrix is the scoring layer on top: your attributes from icp.md, weighted, so accounts come out ranked instead of alphabetical.

Build both manually the first time. This is important because you're essentially deciding what "good" means. And that judgment is what your AI will learn from and benchmark against.

4. Turn one job into one skill.

A skill is codified judgment for a single job, and it must contain: what the job is, what good looks like, what to do when it isn't good, and the number you'd act on.

Take creative fatigue, for example. The skill names the metric you watch, the threshold that counts as fatigued, and what happens when it crosses.

→ If the description of your skill needs an "and", it's two skills. Split it.

5. Run it read-only until the diff matches what you'd have done by hand.

Let it share the copy variations and the list it would build. Then write down what you would have done, and compare.

6. Wire the handoffs so it acts instead of answering.

Use Hooks. They make Claude act across the tools you already pay for:

→ Claude finishes a task → Slack gets pinged
→ Claude enriches a lead → your CRM updates
→ Claude writes a sequence → loaded into @InstantlyAI

7. Keep a human on the last step & feed both outcomes back.

Remember, whenever you review, a mistake or error shouldn't get corrected in the chat.

That fix dies right there with the session.

Open the file that caused it instead and change the line, so the next run picks it up. Same when a campaign wins: the angle goes into angles.md and the list definition into results.md.

This is the only reason run 10 beats run 1.

Your mailbox can sit at a 99 health score while every campaign it sends lands in spam.

We run 80 of them. For most of last year, checking them meant opening a dashboard, one client at a time, whenever someone remembered to.

So we gave Claude Code API access to the entire cold email stack. Here's the full workflow (with an example prompt):

1. The prompt

"run a deliverability check on Acme"

Ninety seconds later every mailbox and every campaign is on one screen, worst first, in three buckets: PAUSE, WATCH, OK.

You work it top down.

2. The three layers under it

- https://t.co/sXUa94GW1L buys the domains, writes the DNS and creates the mailboxes over API, in four to six hours.
- https://t.co/sHzkzBhlen runs the campaigns and the warm-up, and exposes a health score per account over REST.
- Claude Code sits on both, joins them into one row per mailbox and executes the fix.

If you already send through Instantly, the only piece you're adding is the agent on top.

3. The setup we run on every client

- Fourteen days of warm-up before a single prospect sees anything, at 10 a day climbing by 1.
- Leave warm-up running. It doesn't count against your campaign limit, so it costs you no volume.
- Plain text. No study shows the MIME type is a ranking signal, so the gain is in what it keeps out: the remote image, the rewritten link and the CTA button.
- Tracking off, per campaign, under the Options tab.
- That setting doesn't inherit from account defaults, and a duplicated campaign carries the old value with it.
- Buy separate registrable domains for the cold sending.
- Google counts subdomain volume against the parent and reports reputation per domain, so a subdomain of your primary puts your real domain on the line.

Skip ESP matching, Google to Google.

Every number behind that advice traces to a cold email vendor's own blog with no seed panel and no test design, and neither Google nor Microsoft documents a same-provider bonus.

Watch your Google and Microsoft pools separately and save yourself the second infrastructure stack.

4. The four numbers we watch

- Bounce over 3%, with a volume floor under it. One bounce in four sends is 25% and means nothing.
- Health score under 90.
- Replies dying on a campaign that was converting. Earliest signal you get, because reply rate is capped by inbox placement.
- Disconnected accounts. A status of -1 fails silently and drags every average you read.

Be careful with that health score. It only measures warm-up placement, and your campaign sends sit outside its denominator entirely.

That's how a mailbox reads 99 while its campaigns land in spam.

Clear 90 as a floor, then run a seed-list inbox placement test monthly. That's the test that tells you where campaign mail actually lands.

5. The fix

Same prompt. Rank every mailbox by bounce and reply rate, keep the volume on the winners, pull the rest in one pass across all 80.

Re-warm them at 10 a day like new mailboxes and let the health score gate the return.

One campaign bouncing points at the list, everything bouncing points at the infra. True, and slow, because you can't see campaign scope until enough campaigns have already bounced.

Read the individual bounce codes instead:

- 550 5.1.8 is your own DNS. Fix the A and MX records.
- 5.7.1 is reputation. Pause the mailbox and re-warm it.
- 5.7.233 is a tenant quota, so your reputation is fine.
- 451 from Mimecast is a greylist asking you to retry. Infrastructure that gives up on it turns a normal handshake into a lost send.

Here's the build order I'd follow, & what to do at each step:

1. Build the folder before you touch an API key

The install is ~20 min, no developer needed. Most people skip the folder & then wonder why run 5 looks nothing like run 1.

Two files, two jobs:

- CLAUDE.md loads on every run. Standing rules only: who the client is, what tone to write in, what never to do, where output goes.
- brain.md holds the GTM substance. You pull it in with @brain.md when a prompt needs it.

→ Keep CLAUDE.md under 200 lines. That's Anthropic's own guidance, & past that adherence drops.
→ Reference @brain.md in every prompt that touches targeting or copy. 9 characters, & it stops the agent inventing its own ICP mid-run.

2. Rank your sources before the first run

Your ICP doc, your campaign notes & your CRM will eventually contradict each other. Rank them & the model stops picking a winner silently while it writes 40 emails.

At the bottom of brain.md:

1. Closed-won CRM data
2. This file
3. Last quarter's campaign notes

→ Rewrite brain.md after every closed deal. Weekly is the floor.

3. Connect the tools

claude mcp add --scope project coldiq --env 'COLDIQ_API_KEY=${COLDIQ_API_KEY}'

→ Single-quote the variable. Unquoted, your shell expands it first & the real key lands in .mcp.json, the file you're about to commit.
→ Always write the "type". A typeless entry gets read as stdio, so a remote entry carrying only a url gets skipped.
→ Edit .mcp.json & a running session won't pick it up. Restart claude, or reconnect the server from /mcp.
→ Never @ your .env. It loads, & the contents go into the prompt & the session transcript. Put a deny rule in .claude/settings.json & hand the agent a .env.example instead.

4. Run these 7 steps, with a checkpoint after each one

1. Detect the signal. Hiring, funding, tech-stack changes, job posts. The filter should name an event that happened, with a date on it.
2. Score & tier. T1 = strong fit with a live signal. T2 = strong fit, no signal yet. T3 = adjacent, watchlist only. Removes ~80% of the manual sorting.
3. Find the contacts against the tiered list, filtered to the personas in brain.md.
4. Enrich & validate. Email first. Phone on T1 only, it runs ~10x the cost of an email lookup.
5. Write the copy per tier. T1 gets its own prompt per account, built on that account's signal. T2 runs a template with one variable swapped. T3 drops into the volume sequence.
6. Route & launch. T1 multichannel with a call task & a LinkedIn touch, T2 and T3 to the sequencer.
7. Analyse & save. What worked goes back in the file, so the next run starts from a better rubric.

→ Approve the plan, review the list before enrichment spends credits, read the copy before anything goes live. Approving it end to end on the first pass is how you find out something was wrong after the mail went out.
→ Pull job posts off the ATS layer. Greenhouse publishes an open JSON board API, Lever exposes public postings per employer. Tech stack comes off the company's own front end via BuiltWith or Wappalyzer. No login, no scraping.

5. Turn every winner into a skill file

Ask Claude to build the same list 5 times from a typed prompt & you get 5 different lists. You never type it the same way twice, & the output tracks the wording.

A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md in it, holding one procedure written down once.

→ When a campaign lands, that sequence becomes a skill the same day. Six weeks later nobody remembers the send window that made it work.
→ If the description of your skill needs an "and", it's two skills. Split it.

6. The commands you'll actually use

/compact on long list jobs, before quality drops.
/clear between unrelated clients, so the last one doesn't bleed into the next.
/model Opus for planning & copy, Sonnet for bulk mechanical work.
/mcp to see what actually connected.

→ @data/input/ gives you a listing & leaves the files unread. Name the file: @data/input/leads-raw.csv
→ Batches of 100-200 rows, /compact between them. Push 1,000 through in one pass & it degrades partway.
→ Keep approvals on for anything that sends. --dangerously-skip-permissions uploads to your sequencer & starts the campaign with no confirmation step.

7. Put your proof where it gets read

Best cold email I ever got ran the sender's own product on me & put the result in the subject line.

→ Do that with something public. Their open role, their tech stack, the page they read.
→ Lead with something they keep. "Want the list of 1,000 HR directors at companies hiring 5+ roles?" beats asking for 15 minutes.

Write from what they engaged with and what the company research found. A like tells you which topic caught their attention; you still need a reason your offer fits.

You can apply this to profile visitors and event attendees too. For newsletter subscribers, start with repeated engagement. Leave the others on the newsletter.

3. If you sell a service, put a sample of the work in the email.

Use the ColdIQ MCP and Explorium to collect what the company sells, who it sells to and what the recipient owns.

Write a few campaign ideas yourself first. Give those examples to Claude, then ask for 3 ideas per company. Review a sample before running the rest of the list.

Each idea should point to something you found about that business. If you can swap the company name and keep the idea, research further.

You can go further with a rewritten post, a redesigned banner or a landing-page teardown. Check whether the original needs improving, do the work, and review it yourself before sending.

If your buyer serves local businesses, use Openmart to find nearby companies that match your buyer’s customer profile. Send 3 relevant businesses with a reason for each. Skip prospects where you can't find enough useful matches.

4. If you're starting cold, build from a result you can prove.

Pick a case study with a specific outcome. Enrich that customer's company in Apollo or Explorium, then find similar accounts.

Check the business model as well as size and industry. A company can look similar in a database and still have no use for the work you did.

Open with the relevant result and offer to send the case study.

Once replies come in, connect Instantly or lemlist to Claude. Classify the positives, objections and “not now” replies. Enrich the responders and look for patterns in who wanted what.

Use those patterns to propose 3 smaller segments. Review them before GetLeads sources more accounts. An objection about timing needs a different response from an objection about the offer.

5. If you're targeting named accounts with ads, use engagement to decide the follow-up.

Build the account list with ColdIQ, Explorium, PredictLeads or Apollo. Create LinkedIn content for the buyers inside those accounts.

Track company engagement through ZenABM or Fibbler. Use ColdIQ to find relevant contacts at engaged accounts, then qualify them before outreach.

Company-level engagement alone doesn't tell you which person saw the ad. Keep that distinction in the copy.

For your highest-priority accounts, combine calls, LinkedIn and email. Keep the account context with the sequence so each touch follows the same conversation.

6. If your buyer is hard to find in a database, identify the public record that reveals them.

The deck includes court filings, aircraft ownership and company ownership registers. Each answers a different targeting question.

For a law-firm offer, a relevant filing can identify the firm, attorney and case. Check the attorney's actual seniority before treating them as the buyer.

For a product sold to independently owned companies, check ownership before buying contact data. Remove subsidiaries when they don't meet that requirement.

Write the qualifying condition first. Then choose the register that can establish it. A broad industry filter won't answer an ownership question.

7. If you sell recruiting, look at the vacancy behind the signal.

Check saved contacts for job changes in Apollo, and use PredictLeads for publicly reported executive hires and departures. Confirm the company the person left, then find their former manager.

Ask whether they plan to backfill the role. A departure gives you a reason to ask, but it doesn't prove they're hiring.

When a job is already posted, have Claude read the full description and identify the requirement that matters most. Offer 3 real, anonymized candidate profiles that match it.

Another play is companies with several openings and no recruiter listed. Verify who's handling hiring before approaching the founder.

Use BuiltWith to find companies where Greenhouse, Lever or Ashby was first detected recently. Verify when they adopted it, then ask about their hiring process. A detection date doesn’t prove a recent install or a hiring surge.

To get the first campaign running, I'd pick the play whose input you already have.

Save its instructions in a file: the starting list, checks, pass/fail rule, contact lookup and message. Give Claude your ICP and examples of good work alongside it.

Have the first run stop after qualification. Review who passed and why before paying for email lookups. Then verify the addresses, check the copy and connect your sending inboxes. The flowcharts use Hypertide for inbox infrastructure and Instantly, lemlist or Expandi for sequencing, depending on the channel.

Keep approval before the campaign goes live. Save the replies and results with the play so you can change the targeting or offer on the next run.

The person who killed your deal might have just left the company.

Your CRM still says “closed-lost.”

I'd have Claude Code check that before buying another list of cold prospects.

We connected Claude Code to folk, our CRM, and the ColdIQ MCP. Alongside tracking our 2,000+ product signups, this lets us work the opportunities buried in our own deal history.

Before building another list, make the CRM show you where you already have a reason to start a conversation:

1. Find a reason to reopen the deals you lost.

Pull your closed-lost deals from the last 12 months. Have Claude read the call transcripts and put the buyer's exact objection beside each account.

Then investigate that objection. If an integration was missing, check whether you now support it. If someone blocked the purchase, verify whether they're still at the company.

Have the agent return the old objection, what changed and the source.

Only draft a follow-up when you can explain why the conversation would be different this time.

Leave everything else parked. “Just checking in” isn't a change at the account.

2. Find out where your best champions went.

Pull the people who helped get your deals approved. Include the person who spent weeks convincing their boss, even if they never signed anything.

Check their current company through the ColdIQ MCP. When someone moves, qualify the new company before opening an opportunity there.

Keep the old deal attached to their history. Your rep should know what you helped them with before writing the first message.

And assign someone to meet their replacement at the existing customer. Losing your internal supporter is worth acting on too.

3. Check whether your ICP describes buyers or just companies you like.

Set aside some closed-won AND closed-lost deals before giving Claude the rest.

Compare company size, industry, tools used and the signals available at the point you would score a new lead.

A characteristic that's just as common in lost deals as won deals doesn't distinguish the two on its own.

If your winners and losers all use the same software, that tool alone shouldn't earn an account a higher score.

Keep the criteria that separate the groups. Test them against the deals you set aside, and check whether winners tend to score higher there too.

If you revise the model, test it on fresh unseen deals before applying it to new leads.

Save the reason beside each score. Your reps need to see which assumption put an account at the top.

4. Turn a closed-won deal into the brief for your next list.

Send the customer's domain through the ColdIQ MCP to find similar companies. Then check what made the original customer a good fit.

If they bought because they needed to connect a warehouse to their CRM, another company with the same headcount isn't enough.

Check whether the same problem could exist there.

Remove existing accounts, apply your ICP criteria and keep the original customer attached to each match.

For the accounts you work individually, give the rep the shared problem and the relevant customer example.

If you can't explain that connection, research further before writing the email.

5. Follow up on what a signup did inside the product.

Our signups land in folk as enriched, scored people and companies. We track API-key creation, first requests and checkout starts.

For your own product, connect the product events to folk first. Then alert the owner when a checkout starts so they can offer help with the plan.

Send inactive signups an example they can run. Have the owner draft a personal note for strong-fit accounts that have started using the product.

Write down the trigger, owner and follow-up before connecting the events. Otherwise, you've built a dashboard that still needs someone to watch it.

Compare users who were still unpaid at the same point after signup. Use only behaviour recorded by then, and give each user the same follow-up window to convert.

If an event is equally common among converters and non-converters, don't treat it as strong buying intent on its own.

6. Give every new record enough context for these plays to work.

Normalize company domains, verify emails and check for duplicates before adding more records. Enrich the empty fields, then apply your ICP score.

We use Claap for call recordings. Have Claude extract the objection, named competitor and next step into fields on the deal, with the transcript linked.

Keep the buyer's words. “Need warehouse integration” gives the reactivation play something specific to check months later.

“Not interested” gives it very little.

7. Ask the CRM which deals need someone to act.

Our Slackbot and company-brain MCP let the team and agents query the same records.

For your first question, try: “Which deals are expected to close this month but have no agreed next step?”

Return the owner, stage, expected-close date and latest buyer conversation for each.

Give that list to the deal owners to agree the next step with the buyer.

Define “expected to close” once, using your stages and dates. The Slackbot and the agent preparing the sales meeting should return the same deals.

To try this, connect your CRM's MCP to Claude Code and pick 5 deals. In folk, deal records require Premium or above.

Ask it to pull the objections and next steps, with the source for each. Keep that first run read-only.

If the answers are missing, connect your call transcripts and fill the fields. Then run the play you have enough data for.

Once the checks work, put changed accounts into the deal owner's queue before the next list-building run.

Include the old conversation and the new evidence, so the rep can reopen it without researching the account from scratch.

- A short video of you explaining how it works
- One "book a call" button
- Proof (a past result, your content numbers, screenshots of happy replies)
- A free checklist or template people get in exchange for their email

Here's what happens to everyone else (full map below):

1. Identify visitors & engagers

We get the name, title & LinkedIn of our anonymous website visitors. In the US that goes down to the person (depends on the state). In the EU, company only.

Then we add everyone who liked or commented on our LinkedIn posts.

2. Enrich every lead with ColdIQ's MCP

For each one, we find out:
- where they came from (an ad, a post, an outbound email)
- how many people from their company showed up
- title, company size, revenue, tech stack
- which pages they visited, and how many times they came back
- which posts they engaged with, and whether they commented or just liked

3. Drop anyone outside the ICP

Students, competitors & job seekers are out before scoring starts.

4. Score the rest with Claude

Tier 1: ICP fit + high intent. They engaged with a post AND visited the pricing page, came back, and several people from their company showed up.
Tier 2: ICP fit, one visit or one engagement.
Tier 3: partial fit, they browsed the blog.

5. Match the speed to the tier

Tier 1 → Slack alert to the rep → outreach goes out the same day.
Tiers 2 & 3 → slower cadence.

Email goes through Instantly, LinkedIn through Expandi.

Visitors get a message that never mentions the visit. Engagers get one that opens with the topic of the post they reacted to.

6. Nurture whoever doesn't book

They go into our other marketing sequences & the newsletter on beehiiv.
